title: Tesla to Sunset the Cybertruck by 2027 as Focus Shifts to Autonomous 'Cybercab'
snippet: Tesla plans to wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas Gigafactory by mid-2027, clearing manufacturing space for its Cybercab robotaxi amid dismal sales for the futuristic pickup.
content:
AUSTIN, Texas — Tesla is pulling the plug on its polarizing Cybertruck. Chief Executive Elon Musk announced that the electric vehicle pioneer will wind down production of the stainless-steel pickup at its Texas Gigafactory around mid-2027, shifting focus and manufacturing capacity toward its next-generation Cybercab.

Musk framed the upcoming production sunset on X as the "end of an era," maintaining that the Cybertruck was the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made." However, the decision follows years of disappointing sales figures and design-related hurdles that severely restricted its market reach.

Dismal Sales and Regulatory Roadblocks

When Musk unveiled the angular vehicle in 2019, he ambitiously projected annual sales of 250,000 units. Reality fell far short of those estimates. According to figures from Kelley Blue Book, Tesla sold just 20,237 Cybertrucks in the U.S. last year, down 48% from 38,965 units in 2024.

Industry experts point to the vehicle's heavy, rigid exterior as a major liability. The sharp-edged design made it virtually impossible to pass pedestrian safety crash tests in overseas markets like Europe. "Anywhere where you have crash regulation that takes into account pedestrian impact, that Cybertruck won't go, can't go," said former Aston Martin CEO Andy Palmer.

Automotive analysts note that while the Cybertruck's design choices hurt its viability, electric pickups across the board have struggled to win over mainstream American truck buyers.

Pivoting to an AI and Robotaxi Future

Ramping down Cybertruck operations allows Tesla to clear floor space at its sole Austin facility equipped to handle specialized EV production, paving the way for increased Cybercab output. The Cybercab—featuring butterfly doors and lacking a steering wheel, pedals, or mirrors—serves as the cornerstone of Musk's strategy to rebrand Tesla from a conventional car manufacturer into a leader in artificial intelligence and robotics.

Tesla began operating a small pilot fleet of Cybercabs for paid rides in Austin in September. However, the company still faces hurdles from federal auto safety regulators, who continue to evaluate whether the Cybercab complies with U.S. motor vehicle safety standards.

Despite the Cybertruck's retirement, internal leaders view it as a necessary stepping stone. "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab," Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill posted on X.
